title: X-LAB AD9 Aero Bike Review - Is Buying Chinese Finally Worth It?

takeaways.text: As ridden, with bottle cages, a computer mount and pedals, it weighed 7.79 kg; the reviewer does not see it as an aero climbing bike.
The geometry is middle-of-the-road, with 73° head and 73.5° seat angles; the 410 mm chainstays make it stable rather than darting.
X-LAB claims a 0.4 W saving over the Canyon Aeroad, which the reviewer says is within the margin of error of their own tests.
As a bike only, it saved 33.94 W against Cyclingnews' rim-brake baseline, against 40.3 W for the fastest bike tested; with a rider it sat mid-field, 6.76 W slower than the fastest.
It rides much like a Giant Propel: unflappable in wind and on bad roads, with the rear wheel planted in sprints, competent on climbs and comfortable enough over rough roads.
The one-piece cockpit cannot be changed at purchase; his 40 cm bar was wider than he wanted for an aero bike.
He swapped to 30 mm tires for comfort and thinks 32 mm will fit.

disclosure: Publication review with Cyclingnews wind-tunnel testing. The test bike came with X-LAB's own wheels and its groupset is not stated, while the candidate's mainland build lists Vision Metron 60 SL wheels.
summary: Cyclingnews tests the X-LAB AD9 aero bike in its wind tunnel and on UK winter roads.
